## What I found

- **Nodes already have parent pointers.** `rb_node_t` has had `parent` since the baseline, and insert, delete and the rotations already keep it up to date. Using it adds no memory.
- **The parent pointer costs 0 bytes in the pool anyway.** On x86-64 the node is 48 bytes; without `parent` it would be 40. `pool_create` rounds sizes up to a multiple of `alignof(max_align_t)` = 16, so both sizes become 48. Either way a slab holds 85 nodes (4080 / 48), and `pool_stats` reports the same numbers. That's a useful point for your reflection. I'll confirm `sizeof` and `per_slab` with a quick check rather than trust my arithmetic.
- **Both functions are currently recursive:** `rb_free_subtree` and `rb_foreach_subtree`.

## Plan (one file: `src/rbtree.c`)

**1. `rb_foreach`: walk up and down using parent pointers.** Morris traversal is the other option, and I'd avoid it here:
- `rb_foreach` takes a `const rbtree_t *`. Morris temporarily rewrites `right` pointers, which would mean casting away `const` on a read-only API.
- If the callback calls `rb_find` or `rb_validate` while the tree is threaded, it would see a broken tree.
- Mutation 4 (copy-on-write snapshots) will share nodes between trees, and Morris would temporarily change nodes another tree is reading.

The walk:
```c
n = leftmost(root)
while (n != nil):        // invariant: every key < n->key has been visited, nothing else has
    fn(n)
    if n->right != nil:  n = leftmost(n->right)
    else:                climb while n is a right child; n = that parent
```
It uses O(1) extra space, never writes to the tree, and does O(n) work in total because each edge is crossed at most twice. It stops at the root because `root->parent == nil`.

**2. `rb_destroy`: rotate the tree into a right spine as it frees.**
```c
n = root
while (n != nil):            // invariant: n roots the only remaining nodes
    if n->left != nil:  l = n->left; n->left = l->right; l->right = n; n = l   // rotate right
    else:               next = n->right; free n (key, value, node); n = next
```
This uses O(1) space and O(n) time, since each rotation moves one node onto the spine for good. It doesn't read parent pointers, so a stale `parent` can't cause a problem during teardown. I won't touch colors or parents, since every node gets freed. `pool_destroy`, freeing `nil`, and freeing the struct stay as they are.

Then I'll delete `rb_free_subtree` and `rb_foreach_subtree`. The diff should be about 40 lines.

- inserts about 10,000 keys in ascending order and walks with foreach;

`rb_destroy` and `rb_foreach` no longer recurse or use the heap, and use O(1) extra space. `make test`, `make asan` and `make memcheck` all pass. Nothing is committed.

## What changed (`src/rbtree.c`)
- **`rb_destroy`:** works through the tree by rotating it into a right spine. While the current node has a left child, it rotates that child up. When it has none, it frees the node and moves right. It doesn't read parent pointers, so a stale one can't break teardown. It now has the NULL guard (`value_free` is only called on non-NULL values), matching insert and delete.
- **`rb_foreach`:** steps from each node to the next using parent pointers. It never writes to the tree, so it stays truly `const`, and the callback can safely call `rb_find` or `rb_validate`. That also keeps it safe for the copy-on-write snapshots in Mutation 4.

## New test (`tests/test_rbtree.c`)
It builds 10,000 keys in ascending and in descending order, on both plain and pooled trees. Every 7th value is NULL. It checks that:
- foreach visits every key in order and allocates nothing;
- the tree still validates after foreach;
- destroy frees each non-NULL value exactly once;
- no allocations are left outstanding afterwards.

There is also a single-node case. No existing test was changed.

One part of the plan isn't in the test: the tree type is opaque, so the test can't reach a tree's own pool to call `pool_stats` and check `live == 0`. The test checks the allocator's outstanding-allocation count instead.

A red-black tree with 10⁶ nodes is at most about 40 levels deep (2·log₂ n). Forty recursive calls take a few KB of stack, well under 64 KB. Here's what the scratch copy with the old recursive code did on this test:

I added the stack watermark test, and unlike the 64 KB test it catches recursion. The current iterative code passes `make test`, `make asan` and `make memcheck`. The old recursive versions in a scratch copy fail it in all three builds. Nothing is committed.

## How it works (`tests/test_rbtree.c`)
1. The 3-node and 10⁶-node pooled trees are built on the main thread, so the cost of building them isn't measured.
2. Each operation runs in its own thread, on a 64 KB stack buffer the test owns.
3. Just before the operation, the worker fills everything below its own frame with `0xCD`. Just after, it finds the deepest byte that changed.
4. The test fails if the 10⁶-node run uses more than a small tolerance beyond the 3-node run. That compares tree heights of at most 2 and at least 20.
5. A calibration job that writes a 2 KB local array must show up as about 2 KB of use. That guards against a broken probe passing every time.

Setting `WM_VERBOSE=1` prints the measurements.

## Measured stack use (bytes, 3 nodes → 10⁶ nodes)

| | foreach, current | foreach, old recursive | destroy, current | destroy, old recursive |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| plain | 0 → 0 | 0 → **904** | 56 → 48 | 104 → **648** |
| ASan | 0 → 0 | 0 → **1368** | 2360 → 2568 | 2328 → **3544** |
| Valgrind | 0 → 0 | 0 → **904** | 0 → 0 | 0 → **616** |

A 0 means the operation stayed within the 256-byte gap just below the painting code's own frame, which the test leaves unpainted.

## Things I had to work around
- **ASan start-up.** In my first version the whole stack was painted before the thread started. Under ASan, the runtime's thread start-up used more stack than the tree code and hid the recursion. Painting from inside the worker fixed that.
- **Tolerance.** Under ASan, freeing 10⁶ keys uses 208 more bytes of stack than freeing 3, so the allowed growth is 512 bytes under ASan and 128 otherwise. Both numbers come from measurements on this machine's gcc and glibc. A different compiler or libc could change them, and if this test ever fails on a different machine, check that first.
- **Valgrind.** Memcheck reported the scan as 73 invalid reads, because it treats memory from finished stack frames as unaddressable. The scan now calls `VALGRIND_MAKE_MEM_DEFINED` on that one buffer first. That call does nothing outside Valgrind. The header is included behind `__has_include`, so the test still builds without `valgrind-devel`.
- **POSIX declaration.** I added `#define _POSIX_C_SOURCE 200809L` at the top of the test file, because strict `-std=c23` hides the declaration of `pthread_attr_setstack`.

The earlier 64 KB stack test is still there unchanged. It now serves as a "works at 10⁶ nodes" check, and this new test is the one that would catch recursion coming back.
